hc3.a:
**`<!doctype html>` is the document type declaration at the very top of an HTML file. It tells the browser to render the page in standards mode, following modern HTML and CSS rules, instead of quirks mode, which emulates old, inconsistent browser behavior. It is not a tag or an element, and it is case-insensitive.**

### Why it exists
In the 1990s and 2000s, browsers implemented CSS differently. When standards-compliant rendering arrived, browsers kept a **quirks mode** for old pages so they would not break. The doctype is the switch: with it, you get standards mode; without it, the browser guesses and usually picks quirks mode.

### What quirks mode changes
- Box sizing: widths may include padding and borders (old IE box model).
- Tables do not inherit font sizes.
- Percentage heights and some inline layout behave differently.
- Various CSS parsing differences.

These cause hard-to-debug layout differences, which is why the doctype is mandatory in practice.

### Old doctypes
HTML 4.01 and XHTML had long declarations referencing DTDs, for example `<!DOCTYPE HTML PUBLIC "-//W3C//DTD HTML 4.01//EN" "http://www.w3.org/TR/html4/strict.dtd">`. The modern HTML doctype is short because HTML is no longer based on SGML DTDs.

### Rules
- It must be the first thing in the document (only whitespace or comments before it, and comments can trigger issues in old browsers).
- `<!DOCTYPE html>` and `<!doctype html>` are equivalent.

### How to check
`document.compatMode` returns `"CSS1Compat"` in standards mode and `"BackCompat"` in quirks mode.

hc4.a:
**HTML5 replaced HTML 4.01 with a simpler doctype, semantic elements (`header`, `nav`, `main`, `article`, `section`, `footer`), native audio and video, `canvas` and SVG inline, new form input types and validation, and APIs like local storage, geolocation and history. It also defined precise parsing rules so all browsers handle errors the same way. Today "HTML5" is simply HTML, a Living Standard maintained by the WHATWG.**

### Main differences
| | HTML 4.01 | HTML5 / HTML Living Standard |
|---|---|---|
| Doctype | long, DTD-based | `<!doctype html>` |
| Charset | `<meta http-equiv="Content-Type" ...>` | `<meta charset="utf-8">` |
| Layout markup | `<div id="header">` everywhere | semantic elements |
| Media | plugins (Flash, Silverlight) | `<video>`, `<audio>`, `<track>` |
| Graphics | images and plugins | `<canvas>`, inline `<svg>` |
| Forms | text, password, checkbox, radio | `email`, `url`, `date`, `number`, `range`, `color`, `search`; `required`, `pattern`, `placeholder` |
| Parsing | browser-specific error handling | standardized parsing algorithm |
| Presentational tags | `<font>`, `<center>`, `<frame>` | removed; use CSS |
| APIs | few | Web Storage, History, Drag and Drop, Web Workers, and many more |

### Living Standard
After HTML5 (2014), the W3C and WHATWG agreed in 2019 that the WHATWG HTML Living Standard is the single source of truth. Features are added continuously: `<dialog>`, `popover`, `<search>`, `inert`, exclusive `<details name>`, `loading="lazy"`, `fetchpriority`, invoker commands (`command`/`commandfor`).

### Interview tip
Mention semantics, multimedia, forms and APIs, then note that version numbers no longer exist.

hc5.a:
**Semantic tags are HTML elements whose names describe the meaning of their content, such as `<header>`, `<nav>`, `<main>`, `<article>`, `<aside>`, `<footer>`, `<button>` and `<time>`. Unlike generic `<div>` and `<span>`, they tell browsers, assistive technologies and search engines what each part of the page is.**

### Why they matter
- **Accessibility:** screen readers expose landmarks (`banner`, `navigation`, `main`, `contentinfo`) and let users jump between them. Semantic controls like `<button>` are keyboard-focusable and announced correctly for free.
- **SEO:** search engines understand page structure, main content and articles better.
- **Maintainability:** code reads like a document outline.
- **Default behavior:** `<details>` toggles, `<dialog>` traps focus as a modal, `<a href>` navigates, `<form>` submits, all without JavaScript.

### Semantic vs non-semantic
- Non-semantic: `<div>`, `<span>`. They mean nothing; use them only for styling or grouping when no element fits.
- Semantic: everything with a specific meaning, including inline ones like `<strong>`, `<em>`, `<code>`, `<abbr>`, `<mark>`, `<time datetime>`.

### Common mistakes
- **Div soup:** `<div class="button" onclick=...>` instead of `<button>`. It is not focusable or announced as a button.
- Using headings for size rather than structure; style headings with CSS instead.
- Multiple visible `<main>` elements.
- Using `<section>` as a generic wrapper; a section should have a heading.

### Rule of thumb
Pick the element that describes what the content is; if nothing fits, use a `<div>` or `<span>`.

### Sectioning content

`<button>`, `<a href>`, `<details>`/`<summary>`, `<dialog>`, `<menu>`.

hc7.a:
**`<div>` and `<span>` are both generic containers with no meaning. `<div>` is a block-level element (starts on a new line and takes the full width by default) used to group larger chunks of content for layout. `<span>` is an inline element (flows within text) used to wrap a few words for styling or scripting.**

### `<div>`
- Default `display: block`.
- Groups sections, cards, layout wrappers, grid and flex containers.
- Can contain almost any flow content.

### `<span>`
- Default `display: inline`.
- Wraps part of a text: a colored word, a badge inside a sentence, a highlighted price.
- Must contain only phrasing (inline) content; putting a `<div>` inside a `<span>` is invalid.

### Both are non-semantic
Screen readers and search engines treat them as plain containers. Before reaching for them, check whether a semantic element fits:
- Instead of `<div class="header">`, use `<header>`.
- Instead of `<div onclick>` acting as a button, use `<button>`.
- Instead of `<span class="bold">` for important text, use `<strong>`.
- Instead of `<span class="date">`, use `<time datetime>`.

### Display can be changed
CSS can make a `<span>` behave like a block (`display: block`) or a `<div>` inline (`display: inline-flex`), but the content model rules (what may go inside) stay the same.

### Interview tip
Say "block vs inline", "both non-semantic", and "prefer semantic elements first".

hc9.a:
**`<meta>` is a void element inside `<head>` that provides metadata about the document which is not displayed on the page: the character encoding, viewport settings for mobile, the description shown in search results, social sharing information (Open Graph), theme colors, and instructions for crawlers.**

### Common meta tags
- `<meta charset="utf-8">`: character encoding; should be the first element in `<head>`.
- `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">`: responsive layout on mobile.
- `<meta name="description" content="...">`: page summary, often used as the search snippet.
- `<meta name="robots" content="noindex, nofollow">`: crawler instructions.
- `<meta name="theme-color" content="#4f46e5" media="(prefers-color-scheme: light)">`: browser UI color.
- `<meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark">`: tells the browser the page supports both, so default form controls and scrollbars match before CSS loads.
- `<meta property="og:title">`, `og:description`, `og:image`, `og:url`: link previews on social apps and chat tools.
- `<meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">`.
- `<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" content="...">`: a CSP fallback when you cannot set headers.

### Attributes
- `name` + `content` for named metadata.
- `property` + `content` for Open Graph (RDFa).
- `http-equiv` + `content` to emulate HTTP headers.
- `charset` for encoding.

### Things meta does not do anymore
`<meta name="keywords">` is ignored by major search engines. `<meta http-equiv="refresh">` redirects are bad for accessibility and SEO; use server redirects.

### Frameworks
Next.js's Metadata API, React 19's built-in `<title>` and `<meta>` hoisting, and similar tools generate these tags for you.

hc10.q: What is the viewport meta tag?
hc10.a:
**The viewport meta tag, `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">`, tells mobile browsers to use the device's actual width as the layout width and not to zoom out. Without it, phones render the page as if it were about 980px wide and shrink it, so text is tiny and media queries do not work as expected.**

### Why it is needed
Early mobile browsers assumed sites were built for desktops. They laid pages out on a virtual 980px viewport and zoomed out to fit. The viewport tag opts your responsive design out of that behavior.

### Common values
- `width=device-width`: layout viewport equals the screen width in CSS pixels.
- `initial-scale=1`: no zoom on load.
- `viewport-fit=cover`: extend into the notch and rounded-corner areas on phones; then pad content with `env(safe-area-inset-*)`.
- `interactive-widget=resizes-content`: makes the layout viewport shrink when the on-screen keyboard opens (supported in Chromium and Firefox).

### Avoid
- `maximum-scale=1` or `user-scalable=no`: blocks pinch-zoom, which fails accessibility guidelines (WCAG 1.4.4 Resize Text). Modern iOS ignores it for accessibility reasons anyway.
- Fixed widths like `width=600`.

### Related CSS
- Viewport units `vw`, `vh`, and the newer `svh`, `lvh` and `dvh` (small, large and dynamic viewport heights), which handle mobile browser toolbars.
- Media queries now match real device widths.

### Interview tip
Explain the 980px default and the accessibility reason not to disable zoom.

hc11.a:
**`<head>` contains information about the document that is mostly not displayed: metadata, the title, links to stylesheets and icons, scripts and SEO or social tags. `<body>` contains all the content users see and interact with: text, images, links, forms and media. Every HTML document has exactly one of each inside `<html>`.**

### `<head>` contents
- `<meta charset>`, `<meta name="viewport">`, `<meta name="description">`.
- `<title>` (required).
- `<link rel="stylesheet">`, `<link rel="icon">`, `<link rel="preload">`, `<link rel="preconnect">`, `<link rel="canonical">`, `<link rel="manifest">`.
- `<style>` for critical inline CSS.
- `<script>` (preferably with `defer` or `type="module"`).
- `<base>` (rare), Open Graph and structured data (`<script type="application/ld+json">`).

### `<body>` contents
- Landmarks and content: `<header>`, `<nav>`, `<main>`, `<footer>`, headings, text, images, forms.
- Scripts at the end of the body (an older pattern from before `defer`).

### Performance details
- Stylesheets in `<head>` are render-blocking, so the page does not flash unstyled.
- Classic scripts without `defer`/`async` block HTML parsing; place them carefully.
- Preload critical resources (hero image, fonts) with `<link rel="preload">` or use `fetchpriority="high"` on the image.

### Parser behavior
If you omit `<head>` or `<body>` tags, the browser inserts them automatically. Elements that cannot be in the head (like a `<div>`) implicitly close it and start the body.

### Frameworks
React 19 lets components render `<title>`, `<meta>` and `<link>` anywhere and hoists them into `<head>`.

hc12.a:
**`<title>` sets the document's title, which appears in the browser tab, bookmarks and history, is announced by screen readers when the page loads, and is usually used as the clickable headline in search results. It goes in `<head>`, is required for a valid document, and should be unique and descriptive for every page.**

### Writing good titles
- Put the most specific information first: `"Edit profile | Settings | DevQnA"`.
- Keep it concise; search engines typically show about 50 to 60 characters.
- Make each page's title unique, matching the page's main heading.
- Avoid keyword stuffing.

### Accessibility
Screen reader users hear the title first; in single-page apps, update it on every route change so users know the page changed (WCAG 2.4.2 Page Titled).

### Dynamic titles
- JavaScript: `document.title = "3 new messages | Inbox"`.
- **React 19:** render `<title>` anywhere in a component and React hoists it into `<head>`.
- **Next.js:** the Metadata API (`export const metadata = { title }`, `title.template`).
- **React Router:** `meta` exports in framework mode.

### Details
- Only one `<title>` per document; it contains text only (no markup).
- It is different from the `title` attribute, which creates a tooltip on any element and is not reliable for accessibility.

### SEO
Search engines may rewrite titles that are missing, duplicated or unhelpful, so it pays to write them deliberately.

hc13.a:
**`<link>` is a void element, usually in `<head>`, that connects the document to external resources. Its `rel` attribute says what the relationship is: stylesheets (`rel="stylesheet"`), icons (`rel="icon"`), resource hints (`preload`, `preconnect`, `prefetch`, `modulepreload`), the canonical URL, alternate languages, the web app manifest and more.**

### Common uses
- **Stylesheets:** `<link rel="stylesheet" href="/styles.css">`, optionally with `media="print"` or a media query.
- **Icons:** `<link rel="icon" href="/favicon.svg" type="image/svg+xml">`, `<link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="/apple-touch-icon.png">`.
- **Resource hints:**
  - `preconnect`: open a connection early to a critical origin (fonts, CDN).
  - `dns-prefetch`: resolve DNS only.
  - `preload`: fetch a resource needed soon on this page (`as="font"`, `as="image"`, with `crossorigin` for fonts).
  - `modulepreload`: preload JavaScript modules.
  - `prefetch`: low-priority fetch for a likely next navigation.
- **SEO:** `<link rel="canonical" href="...">`, `<link rel="alternate" hreflang="fr" href="...">`.
- **PWA:** `<link rel="manifest" href="/manifest.webmanifest">`.
- **Feeds:** `<link rel="alternate" type="application/rss+xml" href="/feed.xml">`.

### Useful attributes
`href`, `rel`, `as`, `type`, `media`, `crossorigin`, `integrity` (Subresource Integrity), `fetchpriority`, `blocking="render"`, `imagesrcset`/`imagesizes` (for preloading responsive images).

### `<link>` vs `<a>`
`<link>` describes relationships for the browser and is not clickable; `<a>` creates a hyperlink for users.

### Performance tips
Preload only what is needed early; too many preloads compete with each other. Stylesheets are render-blocking by default, which avoids a flash of unstyled content.

hc14.a:
**`<script>` embeds or references JavaScript (or data blocks like JSON). By default a classic script blocks HTML parsing while it downloads and runs; `defer`, `async` and `type="module"` change that. It can contain inline code or load a file with `src`, and it appears in `<head>` or `<body>`.**

### Loading modes
- **Classic (no attributes):** parsing stops, the script downloads and executes, then parsing resumes. Avoid in `<head>`.
- **`defer`:** downloads in parallel, runs after the document is parsed, in order. Good default for app scripts.
- **`async`:** downloads in parallel, runs as soon as it is ready (order not guaranteed). Good for independent scripts like analytics.
- **`type="module"`:** ES modules; deferred by default, strict mode, supports `import`/`export`, scoped variables. Add `async` to run as soon as ready.
- **`nomodule`:** fallback for very old browsers that do not support modules (rarely needed today).

### Other attributes
- `crossorigin`, `integrity` (Subresource Integrity for CDN files), `referrerpolicy`, `nonce` (for Content Security Policy), `fetchpriority`, `blocking="render"`.
- `type="importmap"`: map bare module specifiers to URLs.
- `type="application/ld+json"`: structured data for search engines.
- `type="speculationrules"`: prerender or prefetch likely next pages (Chromium).

### Best practices
- Prefer `defer` or modules for scripts in `<head>`.
- Keep inline scripts small; move code to files that can be cached.
- Avoid `document.write`.
- Load third-party scripts with `async` and consider their performance and security cost.

hc15.a:
**Both `defer` and `async` download an external script in parallel without blocking HTML parsing. A `defer` script runs after the whole document has been parsed, just before `DOMContentLoaded`, and deferred scripts run in document order. An `async` script runs as soon as it finishes downloading, which can interrupt parsing, and async scripts run in whatever order they arrive.**

### Timeline
- **No attribute:** parse, stop, download, execute, continue parsing.
- **`async`:** parse while downloading, stop briefly to execute when ready, continue.
- **`defer`:** parse while downloading, finish parsing, then execute in order.

### When to use which
| | `defer` | `async` |
|---|---|---|
| Execution time | after parsing, before `DOMContentLoaded` | as soon as downloaded |
| Order | preserved | not guaranteed |
| DOM available | yes, fully parsed | maybe not |
| Good for | app code, scripts that depend on each other or on the DOM | independent scripts: analytics, ads, widgets |

### Modules
`<script type="module">` behaves like `defer` by default. `<script type="module" async>` runs as soon as the module and its imports are ready.

### Notes
- Both only apply to external scripts with `src` (except `async` on modules, which also works inline).
- Scripts inserted dynamically with JavaScript are async by default.
- `DOMContentLoaded` waits for deferred scripts but not for async ones.
- With both attributes, modern browsers use `async`.

### Performance
Putting `defer` scripts in `<head>` lets the browser discover and download them early while still not blocking rendering, which is better than placing classic scripts at the end of `<body>`.

**The `<a>` (anchor) element creates a hyperlink to another page, a file, a location within the page (`#id`), an email address (`mailto:`) or a phone number (`tel:`). It needs an `href` to be a real, keyboard-focusable link. Links navigate; buttons perform actions.**

### Key attributes
- **`href`:** the destination (absolute or relative URL, `#fragment`, `mailto:`, `tel:`).
- **`target="_blank"`:** open in a new tab. Modern browsers imply `rel="noopener"`, but adding `rel="noopener noreferrer"` is still common and harmless.
- **`rel`:** relationship: `noopener`, `noreferrer`, `nofollow`, `sponsored`, `ugc`, `external`, `me`.
- **`download`:** download the file instead of navigating (same-origin or `blob:`/`data:` URLs).
- **`hreflang`, `type`, `referrerpolicy`, `ping`.**

### Accessibility
- Link text must make sense out of context: "Read the pricing guide", not "click here".
- Warn users when a link opens a new tab or downloads a file.
- Do not use `<a>` without `href` as a button, or a `<div>` as a link.
- Visible focus styles and enough color contrast; do not rely on color alone to identify links in text.

### Links vs buttons
- Navigation to a URL: `<a href>`.
- Actions (submit, open a modal, toggle): `<button>`.

### Fragments and scrolling
`href="#pricing"` scrolls to `id="pricing"`. CSS `scroll-behavior: smooth` and `scroll-margin-top` (to offset sticky headers) improve this. Text fragments (`#:~:text=...`) can link to specific text in Chromium and Safari.

**An absolute URL contains the full address, including the scheme and host (`https://example.com/docs/guide.html`), and points to the same place from anywhere. A relative URL is resolved against the current document's URL (or a `<base>` element): `guide.html`, `../images/logo.png` or root-relative `/docs/guide.html`.**

### Types of relative URLs
- **Document-relative:** `about.html` or `./about.html` (same folder), `../index.html` (parent folder).
- **Root-relative:** `/images/logo.png`, resolved from the site's origin. The most common choice in web apps.
- **Protocol-relative:** `//cdn.example.com/lib.js` uses the current scheme; outdated now that everything is HTTPS, so use `https://` explicitly.
- **Fragment-only:** `#section` scrolls within the page.
- **Query-only:** `?page=2` keeps the path and changes the query.

### When to use which
- **Absolute:** links to other sites, canonical URLs, Open Graph images, sitemaps, emails and RSS feeds (content viewed outside your site).
- **Root-relative:** internal links and assets in most apps; they survive moving pages between folders and changing domains.
- **Document-relative:** static sites that may be hosted under different subpaths, documentation folders, local files.

### Resolution rules
`new URL("../img/a.png", "https://example.com/blog/post/")` gives `https://example.com/blog/img/a.png`. A trailing slash on the base changes the result, which is a common source of broken links.

### `<base>`
`<base href="https://example.com/app/">` changes how all relative URLs on the page resolve. It is easy to misuse, so prefer explicit paths.

- **`method`:** `get` (data in the query string, for searches and filters) or `post` (data in the body, for changes). `dialog` closes a parent `<dialog>`.

2. Constraint validation runs (`required`, `type`, `pattern`, `min`/`max`).

- `form.reset()` restores default values.

**`placeholder` shows a short hint inside an empty text-like input or textarea, such as an example format (`name@example.com`), and disappears as soon as the user types. It is a hint, not a label: it should never replace a visible `<label>`, because it vanishes during typing, often has poor contrast, and is not reliably announced by assistive technology.**

- Example values: `placeholder="e.g. 2026-11-21"` or `"+91 98765 43210"`.
- Short hints in a search box that also has a (possibly visually hidden) label.

- Users forget what the field was for once they start typing.
- Light gray text often fails contrast requirements (WCAG 1.4.3).
- Some users mistake placeholder text for a prefilled value and skip the field.
- Translation tools and some screen readers handle it inconsistently.

Put format rules or requirements in helper text below the field, linked with `aria-describedby`.

**`required` is a boolean attribute that marks a form control as mandatory. The browser blocks submission if the field is empty, focuses the first invalid field, shows a native message, and exposes the requirement to assistive technology. - **Checkbox:** must be checked (consent boxes).
- **Radio group:** one option must be selected.
- **`<select>`:** the first option must have an empty `value` to act as a placeholder ("Choose…").
- **File inputs:** a file must be chosen.

**`pattern` specifies a regular expression that the value of a text-like input (`text`, `tel`, `email`, `url`, `password`, `search`) must fully match for the form to be valid. It is anchored automatically, so `pattern="[0-9]{6}"` means exactly six digits. Pair it with a clear hint and a `title` or custom message, because the default error is generic.**

### Rules
- The whole value must match: browsers wrap it as `^(?:pattern)$`.
- Since 2023, browsers compile it with the `v` flag (Unicode sets), so some characters must be escaped inside character classes, such as `-` at certain positions, or the pattern is ignored. Test patterns in the browser.
- Empty values are not checked by `pattern`; add `required` if the field must be filled.
- No flags allowed (case-insensitive matching is not available; include both cases).

### Examples
- Indian PIN code: `[1-9][0-9]{5}`.
- Username: `[a-z0-9_]{3,16}`.
- Hex color: `#[0-9a-fA-F]{6}`.
- Strong password hint: `(?=.*\d)(?=.*[a-z])(?=.*[A-Z]).{12,}`.

### Messages
- `title` text is shown in some browsers as part of the error tooltip.
- Better: helper text visible near the field, and `setCustomValidity()` for a specific message in the `invalid` event.
- Style with `:user-invalid`.

### When not to use it
- For emails and URLs, prefer `type="email"` and `type="url"`.
- For numbers with ranges, `type="number"` with `min`/`max`, or `inputmode="numeric"` plus `pattern` for codes.
- For complex rules (dates, cross-field checks), validate in JavaScript and on the server.

- `<caption>`: the table's title; it is the table's accessible name.
- `<thead>` / `<tbody>` / `<tfoot>`: group rows. Browsers can repeat `<thead>` on every printed page.
- `<tr>`: a row.
- `<th scope="col">` / `<th scope="row">`: header cells; `scope` tells assistive tech which cells they describe.
- `<td>`: data cells. `colspan` and `rowspan` merge cells.
- `<colgroup>` / `<col>`: style whole columns (width, background).

### Accessibility
Screen readers announce the matching header as users move between cells, but only if you use `<th>` and `scope`. For complex tables with multi-level headers, link cells to headers with `headers="id1 id2"`.

### Styling tips
- `border-collapse: collapse` merges double borders.
- `table-layout: fixed` makes column widths predictable and rendering faster.
- Wrap wide tables in a container with `overflow-x: auto` so they scroll on mobile instead of breaking the layout.
- Zebra striping: `tbody tr:nth-child(even)`.

**An `<iframe>` (inline frame) embeds another HTML document inside the current page, for example a YouTube video, a map, a payment widget or a sandboxed preview. The embedded page has its own window, DOM, CSS and JavaScript, isolated from the parent by the same-origin policy.**

### Key attributes
- `src` / `srcdoc`: the URL to load, or inline HTML.
- `title`: required for accessibility; it names the frame for screen readers.
- `loading="lazy"`: defer offscreen frames.
- `sandbox`: applies strict restrictions (no scripts, forms, popups, same-origin access) that you selectively relax: `sandbox="allow-scripts allow-forms"`.
- `allow`: permissions policy for features such as `fullscreen`, `camera`, `clipboard-write`.
- `referrerpolicy`: controls what referrer the frame receives.

### Security
- **Embedding others:** always sandbox untrusted content. Never combine `allow-scripts` with `allow-same-origin` for same-origin content, because the frame could then remove its own sandbox.
- **Being embedded (clickjacking):** protect your own pages with `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self'` (or the older `X-Frame-Options: DENY`).

### Communication
Cross-origin frames talk to the parent only via `window.postMessage`; always check `event.origin` on the receiving side.

### Downsides
Each iframe is a full document, so they cost memory and load time, and they can hurt performance if overused.

**`<canvas>` is a bitmap drawing surface that you paint on with JavaScript, using the 2D context (`getContext("2d")`) or GPU APIs (WebGL, WebGPU). It is ideal for games, charts with thousands of points, image editing and visualizations, but its pixels have no DOM, so content is not accessible or searchable by default.**

### How it works
1. Add `<canvas width="300" height="150">` (the attributes set the drawing-buffer size).
2. Get a context: `const ctx = canvas.getContext("2d")`.
3. Draw imperatively: `fillRect`, `arc`, `lineTo`, `fillText`, `drawImage`.
4. To animate, clear and redraw each frame inside `requestAnimationFrame`.

### Canvas vs SVG
| | Canvas | SVG |
|---|---|---|
| Model | Immediate mode pixels | Retained DOM elements |
| Scales | Blurs when scaled | Crisp at any size |
| Many objects | Fast (10k+ points) | Slows with many nodes |
| Events/a11y | Manual hit-testing | Per-element events, accessible |

### Gotchas
- **HiDPI blur:** multiply the buffer by `devicePixelRatio` and scale the context.
- CSS width/height stretch the bitmap; they do not resize the buffer.
- Drawing cross-origin images without CORS "taints" the canvas, blocking `toDataURL`.
- Provide a text alternative (fallback content inside the tag, `role="img"` and `aria-label`).

### Performance
`OffscreenCanvas` moves drawing into a Web Worker, keeping the main thread free.

  const dpr = window.devicePixelRatio || 1;
  canvas.width = 300 * dpr;   // sharp on retina screens

  ctx.scale(dpr, dpr);

    if (y < 14 || y > 136) vy *= -1;

**Accessibility (a11y, "a" + 11 letters + "y") means building websites that everyone can perceive, understand, navigate and interact with, including people who use screen readers, keyboards only, voice control, magnification, or who have color blindness, cognitive or motor disabilities. The standard is WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines), currently 2.2, with level AA as the usual legal target.**

### The four WCAG principles (POUR)
- **Perceivable:** text alternatives (`alt`), captions, sufficient color contrast (4.5:1 for body text).
- **Operable:** everything works with a keyboard, visible focus, no keyboard traps, enough time.
- **Understandable:** clear labels, predictable behavior, helpful error messages.
- **Robust:** valid, semantic markup that assistive technologies can interpret.

### High-impact practices
- Use semantic HTML first: `<button>`, `<a href>`, `<label>`, headings in order, landmarks.
- Every form control has a visible `<label>`.
- Do not convey information by color alone.
- Keep a visible `:focus-visible` outline.
- Respect `prefers-reduced-motion`.
- Add a "Skip to content" link.

### Testing
Automated tools (axe, Lighthouse) find roughly a third of issues. Also test with a keyboard (Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, Esc) and a screen reader (VoiceOver, NVDA).

### Why it matters
It is a legal requirement in many places (ADA, the European Accessibility Act), it improves SEO and usability for everyone, and roughly 1 in 6 people live with a disability.

**ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) is a set of HTML attributes, `role`, `aria-*` states and properties, that tell assistive technologies what a custom widget is, what state it is in and how it relates to other elements. ARIA changes only the accessibility tree; it adds no behavior, focus or keyboard support.**

### Three kinds of attributes
- **Roles:** what something is: `role="dialog"`, `"tablist"`, `"tab"`, `"alert"`, `"switch"`.
- **States:** values that change: `aria-expanded`, `aria-checked`, `aria-selected`, `aria-disabled`, `aria-busy`.
- **Properties:** relationships and descriptions: `aria-label`, `aria-labelledby`, `aria-describedby`, `aria-controls`, `aria-live`.

### The first rule of ARIA
**Do not use ARIA if a native element does the job.** `<button>` already has the role, focusability and Enter/Space handling; `<div role="button">` needs all of that added manually. "No ARIA is better than bad ARIA": incorrect roles actively mislead screen reader users.

### When ARIA is the right tool
- Custom widgets with no native equivalent: tabs, comboboxes, tree views.
- Communicating dynamic state: `aria-expanded` on a disclosure button.
- Live regions: `aria-live="polite"` for toast messages and async results.
- Hiding decorative content: `aria-hidden="true"`.

### Remember
If you add a role, you must implement the matching keyboard pattern. The WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG) documents the expected behavior for each widget.

hc33.a:
**`aria-label` gives an element an accessible name as a string, which screen readers announce instead of (or in the absence of) visible text. Use it when an interactive element has no visible text label, such as an icon-only button, a search field without a visible label, or a second `<nav>` that needs distinguishing.**

### How accessible names are chosen (simplified priority)
1. `aria-labelledby` (references other elements' text)
2. `aria-label`
3. Native labeling: `<label for>`, `alt`, `<caption>`, `<legend>`, or the element's own text content
4. `title` (last resort)

So `aria-label` overrides the visible text of a button, which can confuse voice-control users if the two differ.

### Good uses
- `<button aria-label="Close dialog">✕</button>`
- `<nav aria-label="Breadcrumb">` and `<nav aria-label="Primary">` to tell landmarks apart.
- `<input type="search" aria-label="Search products">` when the design has no visible label (a visible `<label>` is still better).

### Pitfalls
- **Prefer visible text.** Labels help everyone, not just screen reader users.
- If visible text exists, the accessible name should contain it (WCAG 2.5.3 Label in Name): visible "Buy" should not be labeled "Purchase item".
- It does not work reliably on non-interactive elements without a role, like a plain `<div>` or `<span>`.
- It is not translated by some auto-translation tools.
- Use `aria-labelledby` when the label already exists on screen, and `aria-describedby` for extra hints.

**SEO (Search Engine Optimization) in HTML means writing markup that search engines can crawl, understand and present well: a unique `<title>` and meta description, semantic structure with one clear `<h1>`, descriptive links and `alt` text, canonical URLs, structured data, and fast, mobile-friendly pages.**

### On-page essentials
- `<title>` and `<meta name="description">`: unique per page; they form your search snippet.
- **Headings:** one `<h1>` describing the page, then a logical `<h2>`/`<h3>` outline.
- **Semantic elements:** `<main>`, `<article>`, `<nav>` help crawlers find the core content.
- **Links:** real `<a href>` with descriptive text ("pricing plans", not "click here"); crawlers do not follow `onclick` handlers.
- **Images:** meaningful `alt`, explicit `width`/`height`, modern formats.
- `<html lang>` and `hreflang` alternates for multilingual sites.

### Technical tags
- `<link rel="canonical">` resolves duplicate URLs.
- `<meta name="robots" content="noindex">` keeps pages out of results.
- **Open Graph / Twitter tags** control social previews (not ranking, but click-through).
- **JSON-LD structured data** (`<script type="application/ld+json">`) enables rich results: breadcrumbs, articles, products, FAQs.

### Beyond markup
Server-rendered or statically generated HTML (rather than content rendered only on the client), Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS), `sitemap.xml`, `robots.txt` and HTTPS all influence how well pages are indexed.

### Interview tip
Explain that search engines reward helpful content first; HTML makes that content discoverable.

**A meta description is a short summary of a page written in `<meta name="description" content="...">` inside `<head>`. It is not a direct ranking factor, but search engines often display it as the snippet under your title, so a clear, compelling description improves click-through rate.**

### Writing a good one
- **Length:** about 120 to 160 characters; longer text is truncated (truncation depends on pixel width, not character count).
- **Unique per page.** Duplicates across pages waste the opportunity and may be ignored.
- **Summarize the page honestly** and include the main topic naturally; matching query words are often bolded in results.
- **Add a reason to click:** a benefit, a number or a call to action ("Free shipping", "Updated for 2026").
- Avoid quotation marks that end the attribute early, and avoid keyword stuffing.

### What search engines do with it
Google rewrites the snippet in many cases, choosing text from the page that better matches the query. A well-written description still increases the chance yours is used.

### Related tags
- `og:description` / `twitter:description` control link previews in social apps and chat; they can reuse the same text.
- In frameworks: Next.js `export const metadata = { description }`, or React 19 rendering `<meta name="description">` directly in a component.

### Interview tip
Mention the distinction: the `<title>` influences ranking and is the headline; the description mainly influences whether people click.

**A favicon is the small icon that represents a site in browser tabs, bookmarks, history, search results and home screens. You declare it with `<link rel="icon">` in `<head>`; browsers also look for `/favicon.ico` at the site root automatically.**

### A modern, minimal setup

- Design for tiny sizes: a bold, simple mark, not a full logo with text.
- Give the SVG favicon padding and good contrast on both light and dark tab bars.
- Browsers cache favicons aggressively; change the file name or add a query string when you update it.

**`data-*` attributes let you store custom, private data on any HTML element, for example `data-user-id="42"` or `data-state="open"`. JavaScript reads them through the `element.dataset` object (with names converted to camelCase), and CSS can target them with attribute selectors.**

### Rules
- The name after `data-` must be lowercase and may contain hyphens: `data-product-sku`.
- Values are always **strings**; convert numbers and booleans yourself (`Number(el.dataset.price)`).
- `el.dataset.productSku` maps to `data-product-sku` (hyphens become camelCase).
- Setting `el.dataset.state = "open"` writes the attribute; `delete el.dataset.state` removes it.

### Common uses
- Attach IDs or config to elements for event delegation: one click listener on a list reads `event.target.closest("[data-id]")`.
- Styling hooks for state: `[data-state="open"] { ... }` (used heavily by Radix UI and shadcn/ui).
- Test selectors: `data-testid` for stable end-to-end tests.
- Passing server-rendered config to scripts.

### What not to do
- Do not store sensitive data; it is visible in the page source.
- Do not use them for data that has a proper attribute or element (`value`, `<time datetime>`, ARIA states).
- Avoid storing large JSON blobs; use a `<script type="application/json">` block instead.

### Interview tip
Mention event delegation with `dataset`; it shows you know how to scale event handling without one listener per element.

**`draggable` is a global attribute that marks an element as draggable with the native HTML Drag and Drop API. Links, images and selected text are draggable by default; for other elements, set `draggable="true"` and handle the drag events to move data to a drop target.**

### The event flow
- On the dragged element: `dragstart` (set data with `e.dataTransfer.setData`), `drag`, `dragend`.
- On the drop target: `dragenter`, `dragover`, `dragleave`, `drop`.
- **Crucial detail:** a target accepts drops only if you call `e.preventDefault()` in `dragover`.
- In `drop`, read the data with `e.dataTransfer.getData("text/plain")`.

### DataTransfer
- Carries typed data (`text/plain`, `text/uri-list`, custom types).
- `effectAllowed` / `dropEffect`: copy, move or link cursors.
- `setDragImage()` customizes the ghost image.
- Dropped files arrive in `e.dataTransfer.files`, which powers file-upload drop zones.

### Limitations
- **Does not work on touch screens** in most mobile browsers.
- **Not keyboard accessible.** You must provide an alternative (move up/down buttons, or a select menu).
- Styling and animation during the drag are limited.

That is why apps often use libraries like dnd-kit or Pragmatic drag and drop, which use pointer events and add keyboard and screen reader support.

### Interview tip
Mention the `dragover` + `preventDefault` requirement and the accessibility alternative; both are common follow-ups.

**`<video>` embeds video playback natively in the page, with built-in controls, captions, a poster image and a JavaScript API (`play()`, `pause()`, `currentTime`), with no plugin needed. You can provide several `<source>` formats and `<track>` elements for captions and subtitles.**

### Key attributes
- `controls`: show the browser's play/pause, volume and fullscreen UI.
- `poster`: an image shown before playback.
- `autoplay`: only allowed by browsers when combined with `muted`; add `playsinline` for iOS.
- `loop`, `muted`, `preload` (`none`, `metadata`, `auto`).
- `width`/`height` to reserve space and prevent layout shift.

### Formats
List `<source>` elements in order of preference; the browser plays the first one it supports: AV1/WebM for efficiency, H.264 MP4 as the universal fallback.

### Accessibility
- `<track kind="captions" srclang="en" src="captions.vtt" default>`: captions are required for meaningful audio (WCAG).
- Never autoplay with sound, and offer pause controls for anything that moves longer than five seconds.
- Honor `prefers-reduced-motion` for decorative background videos.

### Performance
- Use `preload="none"` or `metadata` for videos below the fold.
- Replace animated GIFs with short muted looping videos; they are often 5 to 10 times smaller.
- For long or adaptive streaming, use HLS/DASH (often through a player library or a video platform).

### Interview tip
Mention the autoplay policy: muted autoplay works, autoplay with sound is blocked until the user interacts.

**`<audio>` embeds sound in a page, such as podcasts, music or sound effects, with optional built-in controls and the same media API as `<video>` (`play()`, `pause()`, `volume`, `currentTime`, events like `ended` and `timeupdate`). Without the `controls` attribute it is invisible, which is useful for sounds you trigger from JavaScript.**

### Attributes
- `controls`: show the native player.
- `src` or multiple `<source>` children (e.g. Opus/OGG and MP3 fallback).
- `preload`: `none`, `metadata` or `auto`.
- `loop`, `muted`, `autoplay` (blocked with sound until the user interacts with the page).

### Accessibility
- Provide a **transcript** for speech content such as podcasts (WCAG requires a text alternative for prerecorded audio).
- Never autoplay audio; if any audio plays for more than three seconds, users must be able to pause or mute it.
- Custom players need real `<button>`s with labels and keyboard support.

### Common patterns
- **UI sound effects:** `new Audio("click.mp3").play()` inside a click handler (user gesture required).
- **Custom player UI** built on the media API, with a `<input type="range">` for seeking.
- **Advanced audio** (mixing, effects, visualizers, synthesis): the Web Audio API.
- **Media Session API:** shows track info and controls on the lock screen and in OS media keys.

### Interview tip
Mention that `play()` returns a promise that rejects if autoplay is blocked; handle it with `.catch()`.

hc46.a:
**`<progress>` displays how far a task has advanced, such as an upload, a download or steps in a form. It takes a `value` and a `max` (default 1). Without a `value` it becomes an indeterminate progress bar, showing that something is happening without knowing how long it will take.**

### Usage
- **Determinate:** `<progress value="40" max="100">40%</progress>`.
- **Indeterminate:** `<progress></progress>`, typically an animated bar.
- Text inside the element is the fallback for very old browsers.
- Label it with `<label>` or `aria-labelledby` so screen readers can name it; it already exposes `role="progressbar"` with value information.

### `<progress>` vs `<meter>`
- `<progress>`: completion of a task over time (0 to done).
- `<meter>`: a scalar measurement within a known range, like disk usage, password strength or a battery level, with `low`, `high` and `optimum` thresholds.

### Styling
It is styled with vendor pseudo-elements:
- Chromium/Safari: `::-webkit-progress-bar`, `::-webkit-progress-value`
- Firefox: `::-moz-progress-bar`

The simplest cross-browser theming is often just `accent-color`.

### Real-world progress
- `fetch` uploads do not report progress yet in most browsers; use `XMLHttpRequest`'s `upload.onprogress`, or stream the response body for downloads.
- For long tasks, also announce completion with a live region.

**`<details>` creates a native disclosure widget, a section that users can expand and collapse, and `<summary>` is its always-visible, clickable heading. It works with the keyboard, is announced correctly by screen readers and needs no JavaScript, making it ideal for FAQs, accordions and "show more" sections.**

### Features
- The `open` attribute controls (and reflects) the expanded state.
- The `toggle` event fires whenever it opens or closes.
- **Exclusive accordions:** give several `<details>` the same `name` attribute and only one can be open at a time (supported in all modern browsers).
- **Find-in-page:** browsers can automatically expand a closed `<details>` when the user searches (Ctrl+F) for text inside it.

### Styling
- The marker is `summary::marker` (or hide it with `list-style: none` and draw your own icon).
- Style the open state with `details[open]`.
- Newer browsers support `::details-content` and `interpolate-size: allow-keywords` to animate the height smoothly.

### Accessibility notes
- `<summary>` acts as a button with an expanded/collapsed state; do not put other interactive elements inside it.
- Keep summary text concise and descriptive.

### When not to use it
For tabs, menus or anything that needs a different interaction model, use the appropriate pattern instead; `<details>` is strictly a show/hide disclosure.

**`<noscript>` holds content that is shown (or, in `<head>`, applied) only when JavaScript is disabled or unavailable. It is a fallback: a message explaining that the app needs JavaScript, a static alternative, or a tracking pixel for users without scripts.**

### Where it can go
- **In `<body>`:** any normal flow content, such as messages, links or a plain HTML version of a widget.
- **In `<head>`:** only `<link>`, `<style>` and `<meta>`, for example a stylesheet that reveals content hidden for animations.

### Typical uses
- "Please enable JavaScript to use this app." in a client-rendered single-page app (Create React App included one by default).
- Showing images normally when a JavaScript lazy-loading library would otherwise never load them.
- Analytics or ad pixels that work without scripts.
- Undoing "hide until animated" styles so content is not invisible.

### Limitations
- It only triggers when scripting is *disabled*, not when a script fails to load or throws an error, so it is not a general error fallback.
- It does not help search engines much; Google renders JavaScript, and server-rendered HTML is the better solution.

### The better approach: progressive enhancement
Build pages that work as HTML first (server rendering, real links and forms) and enhance them with JavaScript. Then `<noscript>` is rarely needed.

### Interview tip
Mention that server-side rendering and real `<form>` submissions are the robust answer to "what if JavaScript does not run?".

**`tabindex` controls whether an element can receive keyboard focus and where it falls in the Tab order. `tabindex="0"` adds an element to the natural Tab order, `tabindex="-1"` makes it focusable only from JavaScript (`el.focus()`), and positive values force a custom order, which you should avoid.**

### The three values
- **`0`:** focusable in document order. Use it for custom interactive widgets that are not natively focusable (and give them a role and keyboard handling).
- **`-1`:** removed from the Tab sequence but programmatically focusable. Used for:
  - moving focus to a heading or `<main>` after client-side navigation,
  - focusing a dialog container or error summary,
  - "roving tabindex" in composite widgets (tabs, toolbars, menus) where only one item is tabbable and arrow keys move between items.
- **Positive (`1`, `2`…):** jumps ahead of everything else and creates a confusing order that breaks as the page changes. Treat it as an anti-pattern.

### Best practices
- Prefer native interactive elements (`<button>`, `<a href>`, inputs); they are already focusable.
- Do not add `tabindex="0"` to static text; screen reader users already have their own reading navigation.
- Keep the DOM order matching the visual order instead of fixing it with tabindex.
- Make focus visible with `:focus-visible` styles.
- Use the `inert` attribute to make whole regions (like content behind a modal) unfocusable.

### Interview tip
Explaining the roving tabindex pattern is a strong signal of practical accessibility experience.

**The DOM (Document Object Model) is the browser's in-memory tree representation of an HTML document, plus the API JavaScript uses to read and change it. The browser parses HTML into nodes (document, elements, text, comments); changes made to the DOM through JavaScript are what update what users see.**

### Key ideas
- **Tree of nodes:** `document` → `<html>` → `<head>` / `<body>` → elements and text nodes. Each node has a parent, children and siblings.
- **The DOM is not the HTML source:** the parser fixes invalid markup (inserting `<tbody>`, closing tags), and scripts can change it at any time. "View source" shows the original HTML; DevTools' Elements panel shows the live DOM.
- **Live API:** `querySelector`, `createElement`, `append`, `remove`, `classList`, `textContent`, `addEventListener`.

### Rendering pipeline
DOM + CSSOM → render tree → **layout** (geometry) → **paint** → **composite**. Changing layout properties triggers reflow, which is why batching DOM reads and writes matters for performance.

### Events
Events travel through the tree: a **capture** phase down to the target, then a **bubble** phase back up. Bubbling is what makes event delegation possible.

### Related concepts
- **Virtual DOM (React):** a JavaScript description of the UI that React diffs to compute the minimal real DOM updates.
- **Shadow DOM:** an encapsulated subtree used by Web Components.
- **Accessibility tree:** derived from the DOM, used by assistive technologies.

### Interview tip
Distinguish the DOM from HTML source and from the virtual DOM; interviewers often probe that difference.

hc51.a:
**CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) is the language that controls how HTML looks and is laid out: colors, typography, spacing, layout, responsiveness and animation. It works through rules, a selector plus declarations, and the "cascade" decides which rule wins when several target the same element.**

### Anatomy of a rule
```
.card { color: #0b1020; padding: 16px; }
```
- **Selector:** `.card`, which elements to style.
- **Declaration:** a `property: value` pair.

### The "cascading" part
When rules conflict, the browser decides in this order:
1. **Origin and importance** (user agent, user, author; `!important` flips the order).
2. **Cascade layers** (`@layer`).
3. **Specificity** (IDs > classes > elements).
4. **Source order** (later wins).

Some properties (color, font) also **inherit** from parent to child.

### What modern CSS can do
- Layout: **Flexbox**, **Grid**, **subgrid**.
- Responsiveness: media queries, **container queries**, `clamp()`, viewport units.
- Logic: **custom properties** (variables), `calc()`, **`:has()`** (the parent selector), native **nesting**.
- Motion: transitions, keyframe animations, **view transitions**, scroll-driven animations.

### Why separate CSS from HTML
HTML describes meaning; CSS describes presentation. Keeping them apart lets one stylesheet restyle a whole site, keeps markup clean and improves caching.

### Interview tip
Walk through how the cascade resolves conflicts; that is the concept most CSS bugs come from.

**A selector is the part of a CSS rule that chooses which elements the declarations apply to. It can match by element type (`p`), class (`.btn`), ID (`#header`), attribute (`[type="email"]`), state (`:hover`), position (`:nth-child(2)`), relationships (`nav a`) and even by what an element contains (`:has(img)`).**

### How selectors are read
Browsers match selectors **right to left**. For `.menu li a`, they find every `<a>`, then check whether it has an `<li>` ancestor inside a `.menu`. That is why the rightmost part (the "key selector") matters most for performance, although for typical sites selector speed is rarely a real bottleneck.

### Selector lists and grouping
- `h1, h2, h3 { ... }` applies the same rules to several selectors.
- `:is(header, footer) a` groups options; it takes the highest specificity of its arguments.
- `:where(...)` groups with **zero** specificity, which is great for easily overridable base styles.

### Good practices
- Style with **classes**; avoid IDs in CSS (their specificity is hard to override).
- Keep selectors short and flat (`.card-title` rather than `.page .main .card h2`).
- Do not rely on deep DOM structure, which breaks when markup changes.
- Use attribute and ARIA-state selectors to style state: `[aria-expanded="true"]`.

Mention `:has()`: it finally gives CSS a way to style a parent based on its children (`.card:has(img)`).

hc55.a:
**Specificity is the weight the browser gives a selector to decide which rule wins when several rules set the same property on the same element. It is compared as three numbers (IDs, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, elements/pseudo-elements); the higher value in the first column that differs wins, and only when specificity is equal does the later rule win.**

### Calculating it (A, B, C)
- **A:** ID selectors (`#nav`).
- **B:** classes, attributes and pseudo-classes (`.btn`, `[type]`, `:hover`).
- **C:** elements and pseudo-elements (`a`, `::before`).
- The universal selector `*` and combinators add nothing.

Examples:
- `a` = (0,0,1)
- `.nav a` = (0,1,1)
- `.nav a:hover` = (0,2,1)
- `#header .nav a` = (1,1,1)

Columns never "carry over": one ID (1,0,0) beats any number of classes (0,15,0).

### Special cases
- **Inline styles** beat all selectors; **`!important`** beats inline styles.
- `:is()` and `:not()` and `:has()` take the specificity of their most specific argument.
- **`:where()` is always zero**, which makes it ideal for resets and library defaults.
- **Cascade layers** (`@layer`) are checked *before* specificity: a simple selector in a later layer beats a complex one in an earlier layer.

### Avoiding specificity wars
Use mostly single-class selectors, avoid IDs in CSS, keep nesting shallow, and use `@layer` to order resets, components and utilities instead of escalating to `!important`.

hc56.a:
**`!important` is a flag added to a declaration (`color: red !important;`) that makes it beat all normal declarations, including inline styles and more specific selectors. It is a blunt override that breaks the normal cascade, so it should be used rarely and deliberately.**

### How it works in the cascade
- Important declarations form their own, higher-priority group.
- Between two `!important` declarations, normal rules apply again: specificity, then source order.
- **Origins and layers are reversed for important rules:** user `!important` beats author `!important` (so accessibility user styles can win), and `!important` in an *earlier* `@layer` beats `!important` in a later one.
- An inline `style="... !important"` beats stylesheet `!important` rules.

### Legitimate uses

**`z-index` controls the stacking order of overlapping elements: higher values appear in front. It only applies to positioned elements (relative, absolute, fixed, sticky) and to flex or grid items, and it only competes within the same stacking context, which is why a `z-index: 9999` sometimes still ends up behind something else.**

### Stacking contexts
A stacking context is an isolated layer; its children are stacked inside it and cannot escape above elements outside it. New stacking contexts are created by:
- a positioned element with a `z-index` other than `auto`,
- `opacity` below 1, `transform`, `filter`, `perspective`, `clip-path`, `mask`,
- `isolation: isolate`, `will-change` on those properties, `contain: paint`,
- `position: fixed` and `sticky`,
- flex/grid children with a `z-index`.

### Classic bug
A modal with `z-index: 1000` inside a header that has `transform` (or `z-index: 1`) can never appear above the page content that has `z-index: 2`, because the whole header context sits at layer 1.

- Use a small, documented scale (e.g. `--z-dropdown: 10; --z-sticky: 20; --z-modal: 100; --z-toast: 200`) instead of random large numbers.
- Use `isolation: isolate` on components to contain their internal z-indexes.
- Render modals and popovers in the **top layer** (`<dialog>.showModal()` or the `popover` attribute), which sits above everything regardless of z-index, or portal them to `<body>`.


**Flexbox (the Flexible Box Layout) is a one-dimensional layout model: a flex container (`display: flex`) arranges its direct children in a row or a column and controls how they are aligned, spaced, wrapped and how they grow or shrink to fill the space. - `flex-direction`: `row` (default), `column`, and their `-reverse` versions.
- `justify-content`: distribution along the main axis (`flex-start`, `center`, `space-between`…).
- `align-items`: alignment on the cross axis (`stretch` default, `center`, `baseline`…).
- `flex-wrap: wrap`: allow items onto new lines; `align-content` spaces those lines.
- `gap`: spacing between items.

### Item properties
- `flex: 1` (shorthand for grow/shrink/basis): share free space.
- `align-self`: override cross-axis alignment for one item.
- `order`: change visual order (does not change tab or reading order, so use it carefully).
- `margin-left: auto`: pushes the item and everything after it to the end.

### Classic one-liners
- Perfect centering: `display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center;`

- Equal-height cards: the default `align-items: stretch`.

Flex items have `min-width: auto`, so long words or wide children can overflow; add `min-width: 0` to the item.

- Navbar with logo left and links right: `justify-content: space-between`.

- For a single item pushed to one side, `margin-left: auto` on that item is often simpler.

**CSS Grid is a two-dimensional layout system: a grid container (`display: grid`) defines rows and columns, and children are placed into the resulting cells, automatically or explicitly by line numbers or named areas. - `gap: 16px` for gutters.
- `grid-template-areas` gives a readable ASCII-art layout.

- `grid-column: 1 / -1` spans all columns; `grid-column: span 2` spans two.
- `grid-area: sidebar` places an item into a named area.

```
grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(220px, 1fr));
```

- **Subgrid** (`grid-template-columns: subgrid`) lets nested elements align to the parent grid, e.g. card titles and footers lining up across cards.
- **Alignment:** `place-items: center`, `justify-items`, `align-self`.
- Masonry layout is being standardized.

### Accessibility
Visual placement does not change DOM order; keep source order logical for keyboard and screen reader users.

**Flexbox is one-dimensional: it lays items out along a single row or column and lets the content decide sizes. |---|---|---|
| Dimensions | One (row *or* column) | Two (rows *and* columns) |
| Approach | Content-out: items size the layout | Layout-in: tracks size the items |
| Wrapping | Each wrapped line is independent, so columns do not align | Items always align to shared tracks |
| Placement | Source order (plus `order`) | Auto-placement, line numbers, named areas, overlapping |
| Best for | Navbars, toolbars, button groups, centering, tag lists | Page layouts, dashboards, galleries, forms, card grids |

- If you want items to line up in **both** directions, use Grid.
- If items should be as wide as their content and simply flow, use Flexbox.
- A wrapping card list where the last row should keep the same widths: Grid (`repeat(auto-fill, minmax(...))`).
- A navbar with logo left and links right: Flexbox.
- Overlapping elements (text over an image) without absolute positioning: Grid (`grid-area: 1 / 1` on both).

Typical page: Grid for the overall layout, Flexbox inside each card or header. Both share `gap` and the Box Alignment properties (`justify-content`, `align-items`).

**A media query applies CSS only when a condition about the device or user environment is true, such as the viewport width, orientation, the user's color scheme or motion preference, or the input type. - `(orientation: landscape)`, `(aspect-ratio: 16/9)`.
- **User preferences:** `(prefers-color-scheme: dark)`, `(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)`, `(prefers-contrast: more)`.
- **Input:** `(hover: hover)` and `(pointer: coarse)` distinguish mouse from touch.
- **Media types:** `screen`, `print` (`@media print` for print styles).
- Combine with `and`, `,` (or) and `not`.

- HTML: `<link rel="stylesheet" media="print">`, `<source media="...">` in `<picture>`.
- JavaScript: `window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)")` with a `change` listener.

- Write mobile-first `min-width` queries.
- Choose breakpoints where the content breaks, not for specific devices.
- Use `em`/`rem` in queries so they respect user zoom and font settings.
- Fluid techniques (`clamp()`, Grid `auto-fill`) reduce how many queries you need.

**Mobile-first design means designing and writing CSS for the smallest screens first, then progressively adding layout and features for larger screens with `min-width` media queries. The base styles are simple and fast for phones, and larger screens get enhancements on top.**

```
.cards { display: grid; gap: 1rem; }                       /* phone: one column */
@media (min-width: 48em) { .cards { grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; } }
@media (min-width: 64em) { .cards { grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); } }
```

- **Focus:** a small screen forces you to prioritize the most important content and actions.
- **Simpler CSS:** adding columns is easier than removing them; fewer overrides.
- **Mobile traffic:** most web traffic is mobile, and Google uses mobile-first indexing, crawling the mobile version of your pages.

- `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">`
- Touch targets at least 24×24px (44×44px recommended).
- Readable base font size (16px) and fluid type with `clamp()`.
- No hover-only interactions; check `(hover: hover)`.

**A CSS preprocessor is a language that extends CSS with programming features and compiles to plain CSS during the build. Sass (with its SCSS syntax) is the most popular; it adds variables, nesting, mixins, functions, loops, partials and modules, which made large stylesheets far easier to maintain before CSS gained many of these features natively.**

### Key Sass features
- **Variables:** `$brand: #2b4bff;`
- **Nesting:** `.card { &:hover { ... } .title { ... } }`
- **Mixins:** reusable blocks with arguments, `@mixin focus-ring($c) { ... }` used with `@include`.
- **Functions and math:** `math.div()`, `color.adjust()`.
- **Control flow:** `@each`, `@for`, `@if` to generate utility classes.
- **Modules:** split code into partials (`_buttons.scss`) and load them with `@use` / `@forward` (namespaced; `@import` is deprecated).
- `@extend` for sharing selectors (use sparingly; it can bloat output).

### Other options
Less and Stylus (older preprocessors), and **PostCSS**, a plugin-based *post*-processor that adds autoprefixing, future CSS syntax, and powers Tailwind.

### Do you still need Sass?
Native CSS now has **custom properties** (dynamic at runtime, unlike Sass variables), **nesting**, `color-mix()`, `@layer`, `@container`, and math with `calc()`, `min()`, `max()` and `clamp()`. Many new projects use plain CSS plus PostCSS, CSS Modules or Tailwind. Sass remains common in existing codebases and design systems that rely on mixins and loops.

### Interview tip
Explain the difference: Sass variables are compile-time constants; CSS custom properties live in the browser and can change with media queries, themes or JavaScript.

**Nesting lets you write rules inside other rules so related styles live together, as in `.card { & .title { } &:hover { } }`. It started as a Sass feature and is now native CSS, supported in all modern browsers, where `&` refers to the parent selector.**

### Native syntax
```
.card {
  padding: 1rem;
  & h2 { margin: 0; }            /* .card h2 */
  .meta { color: gray; }         /* .card .meta (the & is optional here) */
  &:hover { outline: 2px solid; }/* .card:hover */
  &.featured { border-width: 3px; } /* .card.featured */
  .dark & { background: #111; } /* .dark .card */
  @media (width >= 40em) { padding: 2rem; }
}
```

### Differences from Sass
- Native nesting behaves like `:is()`: the parent selector is wrapped in `:is(...)`, so specificity follows `:is()` rules (it takes the most specific selector in a list).
- **No string concatenation:** Sass's `&__title` (BEM-style) does **not** work natively.
- Nested at-rules (`@media`, `@container`, `@supports`, `@layer`) are supported.

### Best practices
- **Keep it shallow (two or three levels).** Deep nesting creates long, highly specific selectors that are hard to override, the main problem with Sass nesting too.
- Nest states, pseudo-elements and media queries for a component; avoid mirroring the whole DOM tree.
- Older browsers need a build step (PostCSS or Lightning CSS can flatten nesting).

### Interview tip
Mention that it is now native and point out the BEM `&__` difference; it shows up-to-date knowledge.

hc93.a:
**Variables in CSS are custom properties: named values you define once, such as `--brand: #2b4bff;`, and reuse anywhere with `var(--brand)`. Unlike preprocessor variables, they live in the browser, follow the cascade and inheritance, and can change at runtime with media queries, themes, component states or JavaScript.**

### Defining and using
```
:root { --brand: #2b4bff; --space: 1rem; --radius: 8px; }
.btn { background: var(--brand); padding: var(--space); border-radius: var(--radius); }
```
- Names start with `--` and are case-sensitive.
- `:root` makes them global; defining them on a selector scopes them to that subtree.
- Fallbacks: `var(--accent, hotpink)`.

### What makes them powerful
- **Theming:** redefine a few variables under `[data-theme="dark"]` or `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)`, and the whole UI updates.
- **Component variants:** `.btn.danger { --brand: #e11d48; }` changes only that button.
- **Responsive values:** change `--space` inside a media query.
- **JavaScript bridge:** `el.style.setProperty("--x", e.clientX + "px")` for cursor effects and animations without recalculating styles in JS.
- **Calculations:** `calc(var(--space) * 2)`.

### Good practice
Use them as **design tokens** (colors, spacing, radii, z-index scale), name them by purpose (`--color-text-muted`) rather than value (`--gray-500`) at the component level.

### Interview tip
Contrast them with Sass `$variables`: compile-time and static versus runtime and cascading.

hc94.a:
**CSS custom properties (often called CSS variables) are author-defined properties whose names start with `--`, read with `var()`. They cascade and inherit like normal properties, are evaluated at computed-value time in the browser, and can be registered with `@property` to give them a type, default value and the ability to animate.**

### How they work under the hood
- They are **inherited by default** and resolved per element, so the same `var(--gap)` can mean different values in different parts of the tree.
- Values are stored as unparsed token streams; they are only validated where they are used. An invalid substitution makes the property "invalid at computed-value time" and it falls back to its inherited or initial value, **not** to an earlier declaration.
- Fallback chains: `var(--a, var(--b, 16px))`.

### `@property`: typed custom properties
```
@property --angle {
  syntax: "<angle>";
  inherits: false;
  initial-value: 0deg;
}
```
Benefits:
- **They become animatable.** Gradients normally cannot transition, but a typed `--angle` used inside a `conic-gradient` can.
- Type checking and a guaranteed initial value.
- `inherits: false` improves performance for frequently changing values.

### Practical patterns
- Design tokens and theming.
- "Private" component APIs: `.btn { --_bg: var(--btn-bg, var(--brand)); background: var(--_bg); }`.
- Space toggles and state-driven styles with `:has()`.
- Passing values from JavaScript: `style="--progress: 0.6"`.

### Performance tip
Changing a custom property on `:root` invalidates styles for the whole document; set frequently changing ones on the smallest element possible.

hc95.a:
**BEM (Block, Element, Modifier) is a CSS naming convention that makes class names describe a component's structure: `.block` for a standalone component, `.block__element` for a part of it, and `.block--modifier` for a variant or state. It keeps selectors flat with low, equal specificity and makes it obvious which styles belong to which component.**

### The parts
- **Block:** a reusable component, meaningful on its own: `.card`, `.search-form`.
- **Element:** a part that only makes sense inside its block: `.card__title`, `.card__image`. Never chain elements (`.card__body__title`); flatten to `.card__title`.
- **Modifier:** a variation of a block or element: `.card--featured`, `.button--small`, `.card__title--muted`. Used *in addition* to the base class: `class="card card--featured"`.

### Why teams use it
- **Flat specificity:** almost every selector is a single class, so there are no specificity wars.
- **No leaking styles:** names are unique by convention, so components do not affect each other.
- **Readable HTML:** you can see the structure and relationships from class names alone.
- **Easy to delete:** all styles for a component share a prefix.

### Drawbacks
- Verbose class names.
- It is a convention, not enforced by tools.
- Scoping tools (CSS Modules, Vue scoped styles, CSS-in-JS) and utility-first frameworks (Tailwind) now solve the same naming and leaking problems automatically, so BEM is less common in component-based apps, though still widely used in design systems.

### Interview tip
Explain the problem BEM solves (global namespace and specificity) rather than only the syntax.

hc96.a:
**CSS Modules are CSS files in which every class name is scoped locally by default: at build time, `.button` in `Button.module.css` is renamed to a unique hash like `Button_button__x7f2a`, and you import the generated names as a JavaScript object (`styles.button`). This gives component-level isolation with plain CSS and zero runtime cost.**

### How it works
```
/* Button.module.css */
.button { padding: .5rem 1rem; }
.primary { background: #2b4bff; color: white; }
```
```
import styles from "./Button.module.css";
<button className={`${styles.button} ${styles.primary}`}>Save</button>
```
- The bundler (Vite, webpack, Turbopack, which Next.js uses) generates unique class names and a mapping object.
- Supported out of the box in Next.js, Vite and Create React App.

### Features
- `:global(.dark) .button { ... }` targets global classes.
- `composes: base from "./shared.module.css";` reuses another class.
- Works with Sass (`.module.scss`) and PostCSS.
- TypeScript types can be generated for autocomplete on `styles.*`.

### Pros
- No naming conventions needed (no BEM), no collisions between components.
- Plain CSS: media queries, pseudo-classes, animations, nesting.
- Static extraction, so no runtime cost, unlike runtime CSS-in-JS (styled-components, Emotion), which is problematic with React Server Components.
- Dead styles are easy to find and delete per component.

### Cons
- Theming across components needs CSS custom properties.
- Class names are less readable in DevTools (configurable in development).
- Dynamic styles need `style` props or custom properties.

### Interview tip
Compare CSS Modules, Tailwind and CSS-in-JS on scoping, runtime cost and Server Component compatibility.

hc97.a:
**Tailwind CSS is a utility-first CSS framework: instead of writing custom class names and stylesheets, you compose small single-purpose classes directly in your markup, like `flex items-center gap-4 rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-4 py-2 text-white hover:bg-blue-700`. A build step scans your files and generates only the CSS you actually use.**

### Key concepts
- **Utilities** map to one or a few declarations: `p-4` (padding 1rem), `text-sm`, `grid-cols-3`.
- **Variants** as prefixes: responsive (`md:grid-cols-2`), states (`hover:`, `focus-visible:`, `disabled:`), dark mode (`dark:`), group and peer (`group-hover:`), `has-[…]:`, container queries (`@md:`).
- **Design tokens:** a consistent scale for spacing, colors and typography. In Tailwind v4, tokens are configured in CSS with `@theme` and become CSS variables.
- **Arbitrary values:** `w-[37rem]`, `bg-[#2b4bff]` for one-offs.

### Pros
- Very fast to build and iterate; no context switching or naming.
- Consistency from a shared scale.
- **Tiny CSS bundles** that stop growing: utilities are reused across the whole app.
- No dead CSS and no specificity battles; styles are local to the markup.
- Works well with component frameworks and Server Components (no runtime).

### Cons
- Long class lists can hurt readability (mitigate with components, `clsx`/`cn` helpers, and Prettier's class sorting plugin).
- Learning the vocabulary.
- Repeated patterns need extraction into components.

### Ecosystem
shadcn/ui, Headless UI and Radix pair with Tailwind for accessible components.

### Interview tip
Address the "inline styles" criticism: unlike inline styles, Tailwind supports states, media queries and design constraints.

hc98.a:
**CSS animations change property values over time using `@keyframes`, which define the steps, and the `animation` property, which applies them with a duration, timing function, delay, iteration count and direction. Unlike transitions, they can run automatically, loop and have many intermediate steps without any state change.**

### Defining keyframes
```
@keyframes pulse {
  0%   { transform: scale(1); }
  50%  { transform: scale(1.1); }
  100% { transform: scale(1); }
}
```

### The `animation` sub-properties
- `animation-name`, `animation-duration`, `animation-timing-function` (`ease`, `linear`, `cubic-bezier()`, `steps()`).
- `animation-delay`, `animation-iteration-count` (`infinite`), `animation-direction` (`alternate`).
- `animation-fill-mode`: `forwards` keeps the final state; `both` also applies the first frame during the delay.
- `animation-play-state`: pause and resume.
- Shorthand: `animation: pulse 1.5s ease-in-out infinite;`

### Performance
Animate **`transform` and `opacity`**; they can run on the compositor without layout or paint. Animating `width`, `height`, `top` or `margin` triggers layout on every frame and causes jank.

### Modern features
- **Scroll-driven animations:** `animation-timeline: view()` or `scroll()` ties progress to scrolling, with no JavaScript.
- **View Transitions API** for animating between pages and states.
- `@starting-style` for entry animations from `display: none`.
- JavaScript control with the Web Animations API (`el.animate()`) and `animationend` events.

### Accessibility
Respect `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`, avoid flashing more than three times per second, and let users pause long-running motion.

hc99.a:
**A CSS transition smoothly animates a property from its old value to its new value when that value changes, for example on `:hover`, `:focus`, or when JavaScript toggles a class. You specify which properties to transition, the duration, the timing function and an optional delay: `transition: background-color 200ms ease, transform 200ms ease;`.**

### Properties
- `transition-property`: which properties (`all` is convenient but can animate things you did not intend).
- `transition-duration`: `150ms` to `300ms` feels responsive for UI.
- `transition-timing-function`: `ease`, `ease-in-out`, `linear`, `cubic-bezier(.2, .8, .2, 1)`, `steps()`.
- `transition-delay`.
- `transition-behavior: allow-discrete`: lets discrete properties like `display` and `overlay` participate, enabling exit animations.

### Transition vs animation
| Transition | Animation |
|---|---|
| Needs a state change to start | Can start automatically |
| Two states: from A to B | Any number of keyframes |
| Runs once per change | Can loop and alternate |
| Great for hover, focus, open/close | Great for loaders, attention effects, sequences |

### Entry animations
Elements appearing (e.g. from `display: none`) have no "before" state; `@starting-style { opacity: 0; }` supplies it, so new elements can fade in with only transitions.

### Best practices
- Transition `transform` and `opacity` for smooth, GPU-friendly motion.
- Put the `transition` on the base state so it animates both in and out.
- Use `transitionend` in JavaScript to run code after the effect.
- Shorten or remove transitions under `prefers-reduced-motion`.

hc100.a:
**`transform` visually moves, rotates, scales or skews an element without affecting the layout around it, using functions like `translate()`, `rotate()`, `scale()` and `skew()`, in 2D or 3D. Because it does not trigger layout, it is the preferred property for smooth animations.**

### Transform functions
- **Move:** `translate(20px, 10px)`, `translateX(50%)` (percentages refer to the element's own size).
- **Rotate:** `rotate(45deg)`, `rotateY(180deg)` (3D).
- **Scale:** `scale(1.1)`, `scaleX(-1)` (mirror).
- **Skew:** `skew(10deg)`.
- `matrix()` / `matrix3d()` for any combination.
- Order matters: `translate(100px) rotate(45deg)` differs from `rotate(45deg) translate(100px)`.

### Individual transform properties
Modern CSS also has standalone `translate`, `rotate` and `scale` properties: `scale: 1.1; rotate: 5deg;`. They can be animated and overridden independently, without rewriting the whole `transform` list.

### Related properties
- `transform-origin`: the pivot point (`center` by default, `top left`, `50% 100%`).
- `perspective` and `transform-style: preserve-3d` for 3D scenes; `backface-visibility: hidden` for card flips.

### Side effects to know
- A transformed element creates a **stacking context** and becomes the containing block for `position: fixed` descendants.
- Its original space in the layout is kept; neighbors do not move.
- It can make text slightly blurry when scaled; avoid scaling text permanently.

### Classic uses
Centering (`translate: -50% -50%`), hover lift effects, icon rotation on open, card flips, and slide-in drawers.
